verdict.reasoning: Patient states: "I can't quite move my left arm. I mean, I can move it, but it's, it's numb. And then I also feel some like tingling in my fingertips."
Patient describes a transient visual issue in the left eye: "I all of a sudden just couldn't see from the... from my left eye. Like, I lost some, like a little bit of a field of vision..."
Patient says: "I've started taking this boxing class. I've been taking boxing class for a few weeks..."
Patient notes: "it's probably been, I'd say for at least two weeks and it's kind of gotten worse... then the numbing kind of started."

Patient says: "I can feel it both in my, you know, a little bit in my elbow and then in my arm as well as in my hand" and later specifies fingers: "it's my second, third and fourth finger" and "it's the... front side" (palm side).
Patient describes symptoms while resting: "if I'm just like resting, if I'm sitting like right now, I can feel like it's numb" indicating rest does not relieve it.
Patient: "I tried massage, I tried some hot baths and that didn't help with this numbness."
Patient: "sometimes I will feel it in my shoulder... if I try to like, you know, move like in boxing and stuff, I will even like maybe feel a little bit of, a little bit of pain."
She notes persistence at rest: "if I'm just like resting, if I'm sitting like right now, I can feel like it's numb and I actually feel tingling right now."

Patient reports mild weakness but not difficulty grasping: "I can grasp a glass. But because I use my right hand most of the time..." and agrees to mild weakness, so stating difficulty grasping adds a feature she denies.

Doctor asks about dropping things; no dropping is implied: "have you been dropping it" and patient instead mentions piano difficulty but does not describe dropping objects; fact accurately reflects "not dropping..." from "So not so much with the glass... I can grasp a glass."
Doctor: "Any neck pain at all?" Patient: "No, not. No neck pain."
Patient: "I all of a sudden just couldn't see from... my left eye... that just lasted maybe for, I don't know, 20, 20 minutes... And then when I... woke up, it was gone."
Patient does NOT deny headaches; she reports them: "Sometimes I get headaches, but I think they're just tired headaches." She only denies seizures: "Oh, no, no, no, no. Nothing like that."

Fatigue described: "Sometimes I get headaches, but I think they're just tired headaches... I'll really just exhaust myself. And then I just kind of feel this fatigue" and "this morning... I just felt really fatigued."
Patient summarises: "But in general, I'm pretty healthy. I mean, I, you know, I work out a lot, and I don't really have any medical problems."
She says: "I do take ibuprofen just because my, my muscles were sore... I've just kind of taken ibuprofen for that." This implies as-needed use.
Patient: "every once in a while I take vitamin D. I take some." and later: "But vitamin D, I take."
Patient: "my GP really wants me to take iron supplements, but you know, there are this like huge pill, so I, most of the time I just forget." This supports that she sometimes takes them.
Patient: "And then sometimes I take melatonin to help me sleep."
Allergies are not mentioned anywhere in the transcript; stating that no allergies are documented correctly reflects missing information.
Patient: "I know that my dad has. I don't know if it's hypo. I think it's hypothyroidism... and then my, like he's got some autoimmune stuff going on."
Patient: "my mom, she's... got diabetes, type 2".
Same section: "my mom... she's got hypertension".
Patient: "my mom... she's got... high cholesterol" which corresponds to hyperlipidemia.
Doctor: "Any neurological conditions in the family? Nerve related conditions?" Patient: "No."
She repeatedly mentions boxing class: "I've started taking this boxing class. I've been taking boxing class for a few weeks" and discusses boxing movements.
Patient: "I was out, you know, drinking with friends... we kind of went crazy and we were like out partying until, you know, late hours, and I just got uncharacteristically drunk for me."
Smoking is not mentioned in the transcript; stating that the patient does not report smoking is consistent with the absence of this information.
There is no description of physical examination maneuvers or vital signs; the encounter is history and assessment only.

As above: numbness and tingling from elbow to hand and 2nd–4th fingers palm side: "a little bit in my elbow and then in my arm as well as in my hand" and "it's my second, third and fourth finger" and "It's the front side."
Weakness described: "So you would say there's a mild weakness? Mild, yes." and difficulties with piano: "it's been kind of harder to get the notes."
Visual disturbance: "I all of a sudden just couldn't see from... my left eye... that just lasted maybe for, I don't know, 20, 20 minutes... and... it was gone."
Neck pain denial: "Any neck pain at all?" "No, not. No neck pain."

Patient denies seizures: "Oh, no, no, no, no. Nothing like that." but she does report headaches: "Sometimes I get headaches". So stating "no... persistent headaches" mischaracterizes that headaches are present, even if she considers them 'tired.'
Symptoms for a couple of weeks qualify as subacute, with numbness, tingling, and mild weakness: "at least two weeks" and "numb" with tingling and "you would say there's a mild weakness? Mild, yes."

Doctor only explicitly mentions MS: "Sometimes, you know, you do get things like ms, multiple sclerosis." No discussion of peripheral neuropathy, neuropraxia, cervical radiculopathy, or other listed etiologies occurs.

While the doctor links symptoms to possible MS and orders urgent referral, the transcript does not explicitly frame it as a concern specifically due to temporal association with boxing nor list that full reasoning; this analytical statement goes beyond what is said.

The transient unilateral left visual disturbance is described and the doctor ties it to possible demyelinating disease and need for neurology: "people with multiple sclerosis can have visual problems like what you've experienced" and "I'm going to do an urgent, very urgent neurology referral."

Doctor treats progression and visual issues as red flags requiring urgent evaluation: he cites vision loss plus arm weakness as reasons to suspect more than boxing and to do an "urgent, very urgent neurology referral" and gives ED advice if symptoms progress.

Doctor states: "I'm going to do an urgent, very urgent neurology referral... What that might entail is the brain scan and things like that." MRI with and without contrast and cervical spine imaging are not specified; adding those details is beyond the transcript.
The transcript only mentions that neurology may arrange a brain scan; it does not state that additional imaging will be considered as part of a broader CNS workup.

Doctor gives red-flag advice: "if the weakness progresses to your legs or there's any kind of headaches, vomiting, fits, and your visual symptoms are getting worse and not getting better, then that would be an A" (implying urgent care/ED).
There is no discussion of continuing ibuprofen as part of the plan; ibuprofen is only mentioned in history of use.
No explicit recommendation is made to continue vitamin D; it is only listed in current medications.
Use of iron supplements is discussed as what the GP wants and that she often forgets, but no plan is stated in this consultation.
Melatonin is mentioned as a current occasional medication, but no plan to use it as needed is discussed during this visit.
While an urgent neurology referral is ordered, there is no mention of follow-up logistics such as ensuring scheduling or documenting results to adjust the plan.
